To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
tailoring display-time thresholds based on task, but not user, information improves IRF performance.
tailoring the display time threshold of IRF algorithms based on task information, rather than on user information, improves retrieval effectiveness.
Tailoring implicit feedback algorithms based on information about the task improves performance, but tailoring based on information about individual users does not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of algorithms that use implicit relevance feedback (IRF) to support the information-seeking behavior of search users.
the development and evaluation of implicit feedback algorithms.
the design of IRF algorithms, and in particular, the effect of personalization and the use of task information on IRF performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the task is the key to the success of IRF.
the use of IRF is a viable approach to personalization, but that the use of user and task information to tailor IRF algorithms should be approached with caution.
task information is important to IRF algorithms, while individual user information is less so.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
task information can improve IRF algorithms' performance, and user information cannot.
the effectiveness of IRF algorithms is highly task-dependent and can be improved by using task information to tailor the thresholds used by the algorithm.
task information is more important than user information when personalizing implicit feedback algorithms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effectiveness of an IRF algorithm can be enhanced by using information about the task, but not the user.
IRF algorithms can benefit from using task information, and that user information is not necessarily helpful.
IRF algorithms should be tailored to the task, and not the individual.
